claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Brody et al., 2013; Staley et al., 2006; and Cosgrove et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Varenicline at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells following 17 hr of exposure.
claims.source: Varenicline (Figure 1A) at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Figure 1B, 'Var', red columns in the left, 'live cells' half of the graph) nor in cortical neurons (Figure 1F, left) following 17 hr of exposure.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Varenicline at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in cortical neurons following 17 hr of exposure.
claims.source: Varenicline (Figure 1A) at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Figure 1B, 'Var', red columns in the left, 'live cells' half of the graph) nor in cortical neurons (Figure 1F, left) following 17 hr of exposure.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: A full concentration-response curve with chronic varenicline revealed an inverted U-shaped dependence of upregulation of binding that peaked at 60–70% of that observed with nicotine at varenicline concentrations between 100 nM and 1 μM.
claims.source: However, a full concentration-response curve with chronic varenicline revealed an inverted U-shaped dependence of upregulation of binding that peaked at 60–70% of that observed with nicotine, which occurred at varenicline concentrations between 100 nM and 1 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, black circles).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Varenicline (30 μM) co-applied with nicotine prevented nicotine upregulation of binding in both heterologous cells and cortical neurons.
claims.source: When co-applied with nicotine, varenicline (30 μM) prevented nicotine upregulation of binding in both heterologous cells and cortical neurons (Figure 1B,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The reversal of the actions of nicotine on α4β2R binding by varenicline was concentration-dependent, with upregulation decreasing exponentially with increased varenicline concentration.
claims.source: The reversal of the actions of nicotine on α4β2R binding also was concentration-dependent, with upregulation decreasing exponentially with increased varenicline concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, black squares).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Varenicline concentrations in the brain are likely to be higher than in plasma because of the presence of high-affinity binding to nAChRs.
claims.source: Recent studies indicate that varenicline concentrations in the brain are likely to be higher than in plasma because of the presence of high-affinity binding to nAChRs (Rollema et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Unbound varenicline concentrations in the brain fall in the range of 32 to 131 nM.
claims.source: Based on this study's estimates, unbound varenicline concentrations in the brain fall in the range of 32 to 131 nM and plasma concentrations are approximately 4-fold lower.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010 study.

claims.claim: Varenicline plasma concentrations are approximately 4-fold lower than brain concentrations.
claims.source: Based on this study's estimates, unbound varenicline concentrations in the brain fall in the range of 32 to 131 nM and plasma concentrations are approximately 4-fold lower.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010 study.

claims.claim: A previous study found differences in varenicline binding to human α4β2Rs compared to rat α4β2Rs when expressed in Xenopus oocytes.
claims.source: In addition, a previous study found differences in varencilcine binding to human α4β2Rs compared to rat α4β2Rs when expressed in Xenopus oocytes (Papke et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Papke et al., 2010.

claims.claim: At 100 nM varenicline, nicotine upregulation was significantly reduced to ~60% of the level without varenicline for both rat and human α4β2Rs.
claims.source: We found that at 100 nM varenicline nicotine upregulation was significantly reduced to ~60% of the level without varencline (Figure 1G) for both rat and human α4β2Rs.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences between rat and human α4β2Rs at 0, 100 nM and 30 μM varenicline.
claims.source: We also found no significant differences between rat and human α4β2Rs at 0, 100 nM and 30 μM varenicline (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Varenicline should reduce nicotine upregulation at concentrations expected to exist in brain.
claims.source: These results indicate that varenicline should reduce nicotine upregulation at concentrations expected to exist in brain.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing effects at 100 nM and estimates of brain concentrations.

claims.claim: Varenicline is unlikely to act as a partial agonist at concentrations expected in brain.
claims.source: In contrast, varenicline is unlikely to act as a partial agonist at these concentrations (Rollema et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Lobeline has smoking cessation activity.
claims.source: Another nAChR partial agonist, lobeline, reported to have smoking cessation activity (Damaj et al., 1997; Miller et al., 2003) had effects similar to those of varenicline (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Damaj et al., 1997 and Miller et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Chronic exposure to lobeline alone or together with nicotine reduced 125I-epibatidine binding levels below that observed for the untreated cells and neurons.
claims.source: Chronic exposure to lobeline alone or together with nicotine reduced 125I-epibatidine binding levels below that observed for the untreated cells and neurons ('Lob', blue columns in the left, 'live cells' half of the graphs in Figure 1B,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The inverted U-shaped concentration-dependence of lobeline effects on upregulation was similar to that of varenicline, with 125I-epibatidine binding peaking at ~50% of nicotine-induced upregulation at 100 nM – 1 μM.
claims.source: The inverted U-shaped concentration-dependence of lobeline effects on upregulation was similar to that of varenicline. 125I-epibatidine binding peaked at ~50% of nicotine-induced upregulation, was maximal at 100 nM – 1 μM, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, black circles), and co-incubation with nicotine reduced upregulation exponentially with increasing concentrations of lobeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, black squares).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: If 125I-epibatidine binding was performed on membrane fragments instead of intact cells, varenicline upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells to the same degree as nicotine and did not reduce nicotine upregulation.
claims.source: If 125I-epibatidine binding was performed on membrane fragments instead of intact cells, varenicline upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells to the same degree as nicotine and did not reduce nicotine upregulation (Figure 1B, red columns on right, 'membranes' half of the graph).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Lobeline exposure upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to about 50% of that observed with nicotine treatment in membrane fragments.
claims.source: Lobeline exposure upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to about 50% of that of observed with nicotine treatment and reduced nicotine upregulation by 50% (Figure 1B, blue columns on right half of the graph).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Lobeline reduced nicotine upregulation by 50% in membrane fragments.
claims.source: Lobeline exposure upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to about 50% of that of observed with nicotine treatment and reduced nicotine upregulation by 50% (Figure 1B, blue columns on right half of the graph).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Previous studies found that chronic varenicline exposure upregulated 3H-epibatidine binding to brain tissue to the same degree as nicotine and reported no effect of varenicline exposure on nicotine upregulation.
claims.source: The effects of varenicline and lobeline on nicotine upregulation were therefore distinct in live cells and membrane fragments, which could explain why previous studies found that chronic varenicline exposure upregulated 3H-epibatidine binding to brain tissue to the same degree as nicotine and reported no effect of varenicline exposure on nicotine upregulation (Hussmann et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hussmann et al., 2012 and Turner et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Previous studies on varenicline upregulation were done with membrane preparations.
claims.source: These experiments were done with membrane preparations, whereas the suppressive activity of varenicline on nicotine upregulation was only observed in intact cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from citations to Hussmann et al., 2012 and Turner et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Nicotine was described previously as being concentrated and trapped in intracellular acidic compartments in Xenopus oocytes expressing α4β2Rs.
claims.source: This process was described previously for nicotine in Xenopus oocytes expressing α4β2Rs (Jia et al., 2003); furthermore, slow release of nicotine from acidic compartments caused α4β2R desensitization, thereby reducing ACh-induced α4β2R currents.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jia et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Slow release of nicotine from acidic compartments caused α4β2R desensitization in Xenopus oocytes.
claims.source: This process was described previously for nicotine in Xenopus oocytes expressing α4β2Rs (Jia et al., 2003); furthermore, slow release of nicotine from acidic compartments caused α4β2R desensitization, thereby reducing ACh-induced α4β2R currents.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jia et al., 2003.

claims.claim: NH4Cl treatment altered the effects of varenicline and lobeline on 125I-epibatidine binding such that both ligands produced upregulation of binding.
claims.source: NH4Cl treatment altered the effects of varenicline and lobeline on 125I-epibatidine binding; both ligands produced upregulation of binding (Figure 1D left half, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C), in contrast to their actions at physiological pH (Figure 1B, leftmost trio of columns).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C.

claims.claim: NH4Cl exposure following co-incubation with nicotine relieved the suppression of upregulation by varenicline and lobeline.
claims.source: Moreover, NH4Cl exposure following co-incubation with nicotine relieved the suppression of upregulation by varenicline and lobeline (Figure 1D, right trio of columns, Figure 1-figure supplement B, D), such that 125I-epibatidine binding in these conditions were indeed similar to the results using membrane preparations (Figure 1B, rightmost trio of columns).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D.

claims.claim: NH4Cl treatment of cultured cortical neurons had similar effects on 125I-epibatidine binding after varenicline or lobeline exposures as in HEK cells.
claims.source: NH4Cl treatment of cultured cortical neurons had similar effects on 125I-epibatidine binding after varenicline or lobeline exposures (Figure 1F, right half of graph).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Incubation with the proton pump inhibitor bafilomycin A (50 nM) produced similar 125I-epibatidine binding results as NH4Cl treatment.
claims.source: We also obtained similar 125I-epibatidine binding results with HEK cells using two other methods to reduce the pH gradient - incubation with the proton pump inhibitor bafilomycin A (Baf, 50 nM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or with the weak base chloroquine (Chlor, 150 μM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Incubation with the weak base chloroquine (150 μM) produced similar 125I-epibatidine binding results as NH4Cl treatment.
claims.source: We also obtained similar 125I-epibatidine binding results with HEK cells using two other methods to reduce the pH gradient - incubation with the proton pump inhibitor bafilomycin A (Baf, 50 nM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or with the weak base chloroquine (Chlor, 150 μM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Nicotine upregulation of currents from α4β2R-expressing HEK cells was observed as an increase by ~5 fold in mean peak current amplitudes.
claims.source: Nicotine upregulation of currents from α4β2R-expressing HEK cells was observed as an increase by ~5 fold in mean peak current amplitudes (e.g., Figure 2A, white vs. black column).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Varenicline exposure alone did not alter nAChR current amplitudes.
claims.source: Exposure to varenicline alone did not alter nAChR current amplitudes, whereas lobeline reduced the mean amplitude to below that of control (untreated) receptor currents.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Lobeline exposure reduced the mean nAChR current amplitude to below that of control (untreated) receptor currents.
claims.source: Exposure to varenicline alone did not alter nAChR current amplitudes, whereas lobeline reduced the mean amplitude to below that of control (untreated) receptor currents.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: When co-incubated with nicotine, both varenicline and lobeline occluded functional upregulation.
claims.source: When co-incubated with nicotine, both varenicline and lobeline occluded functional upregulation; lobeline treatment again reduced nAChR currents to a mean amplitude below even that of the control group.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claims.claim: Neither varenicline nor lobeline treatment changed the time course of desensitization of the ACh currents.
claims.source: Neither treatment changed the time course of desensitization of the ACh currents.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: NH4Cl (20 mM) treatment partly restored nicotine-induced functional upregulation of ACh currents in lobeline and varenicline treated α4β2R-expressing HEK cells.
claims.source: NH4Cl (20 mM) treatment also partly restored nicotine-induced functional upregulation of ACh currents in lobeline and varenicline treated α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Figure 2C,D), albeit to a lesser degree than as observed with the binding experiments.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claims.claim: 125I-epibatidine binding was highly reduced for cells that received the bathing solution from cells chronically treated with varenicline or lobeline as compared to untreated cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the release of varenicline and lobeline from intracellular acidic compartments, 125I-epibatidine binding was highly reduced for cells that received the bathing solution from cells chronically treated with varenicline or lobeline as compared to untreated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Nicotine upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding from live cells was similar to that in membrane preparations.
claims.source: Nicotine upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding from live cells was similar to that in membrane preparations (Figure 1) and following neutralization of the pH gradient of acidic compartments (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Functional upregulation of ACh currents by nicotine did not change if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished.
claims.source: Functional upregulation of ACh currents by nicotine also did not change if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished (Figure 2C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claims.claim: Nicotine is not trapped in the acidic compartment of α4β2R-expressing HEK cells.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with previous findings that nicotine is not trapped in the acidic compartment of α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Jia et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jia et al., 2003 and experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: DHβE is a weak base and a α4β2R competitive antagonist.
claims.source: Dihydro-beta-erythroid (DHβE, Figure 3A) is a weak base and a α4β2R competitive antagonist.
claims.evidence: Supported by established pharmacological knowledge about DHβE.

claims.claim: DHβE was found to induce upregulation of α4β2R high-affinity binding sites.
claims.source: Despite being a competitive antagonist, DHβE was found to induce upregulation of α4β2R high-affinity binding sites (Whiteaker et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Whiteaker et al., 1998.

claims.claim: A 2-fold upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding was observed with 17 hr of exposure of the cells to 100 μM DHβE.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings, we observed a 2-fold upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding with 17 hr of exposure of the cells to 100 μM DHβE (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Acute application of DHβE at 100 μM completely inhibits ACh-induced currents.
claims.source: At this concentration, acute application of DHβE completely inhibits ACh-induced currents (data not shown), as was shown previously (Wu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Prolonged DHβE exposure upregulated ACh-induced currents, similar to the binding sites.
claims.source: Conversely, prolonged DHβE exposure upregulated ACh-induced currents, similar to the binding sites (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: DHβE did not occlude nicotine upregulation when the two ligands were co-incubated.
claims.source: DHβE did not occlude nicotine upregulation when the two ligands were co-incubated, however, demonstrating that it has a different effect on functional upregulation than varenicline and lobeline.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding by DHβE was unchanged whether membranes were assayed or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment.
claims.source: Like nicotine, we see no evidence of DHβE being trapped in binding assays; upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding was unchanged whether membranes were assayed (data not shown) or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment (Figure 3B, green columns in the right half of the graph).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Nicotine and DHβE are less likely than varenicline and lobeline to be trapped because they are less likely to be in their protonated form in an acidic compartment.
claims.source: Based on this correlation between their physical properties and our current data, we propose that nicotine and DHβE are less likely than varenicline and lobeline to be trapped because they are less likely to be in their protonated form in an acidic compartment.
claims.evidence: Inferred from pKa values in Table 1 and experimental data showing differential trapping.

claims.claim: For exposures for 17–18 hr at concentrations up to 100 μM mecamylamine, there was no evidence of upregulation as assayed by 125I-epibatidine binding or by ACh-induced currents.
claims.source: For exposures for 17–18 hr at concentrations up to 100 μM, there was no evidence of upregulation as assayed by 125I-epibatidine binding (Figure 3D) or by ACh-induced currents (data not shown).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Acute application of mecamylamine (100 μM) inhibited ACh-induced currents.
claims.source: Acute application of mecamylamine (100 μM) inhibited ACh-induced currents (data not shown) as previously observed (Wu et al., 2006), confirming that the drug had the expected pharmacological activity.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2006.

claims.claim: There was no difference in mecamylamine binding when performed on membranes or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment.
claims.source: Despite its high pKa value, we observed no evidence of mecamylamine being trapped because there was no difference in the binding when performed on membranes (data not shown) or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Mecamylamine appears to readily cross the blood-brain barrier and cell membranes.
claims.source: However, mecamylamine appears to readily cross the blood-brain barrier and cell membranes (Shytle et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Shytle et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Trapping requires high-affinity ligand binding to α4β2R located within acidic compartments.
claims.source: A more likely possibility is that trapping also requires high-affinity ligand binding to α4β2R located within acidic compartments.
claims.evidence: Inferred from mecamylamine's lack of trapping despite high pKa and its low affinity for α4β2R.

claims.claim: The pKa value and affinity for epibatidine are both higher than those for varenicline and lobeline.
claims.source: The pKa value and affinity for epibatidine are both higher than those for varenicline and lobeline (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: Epibatidine (30 μM) did not promote upregulation of either 125I-epibatidine binding or ACh-induced currents in intact cells.
claims.source: In intact cells, epibatidine (30 μM) did not promote upregulation of either 125I-epibatidine binding (Figure 3C left half, D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or ACh-induced currents (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Epibatidine reduced nicotine-induced upregulation in both binding and functional assays.
claims.source: However, epibatidine reduced nicotine-induced upregulation in both assays (Figure 3C left half, D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: With NH4Cl treatment, epibatidine upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to 60% of the nicotine induced value.
claims.source: With NH4Cl treatment, we observed upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding to 60% of the nicotine induced value and that nicotine upregulation was reduced by 40%.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: With NH4Cl treatment, nicotine upregulation was reduced by 40% in the presence of epibatidine.
claims.source: With NH4Cl treatment, we observed upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding to 60% of the nicotine induced value and that nicotine upregulation was reduced by 40%.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Epibatidine behaves in a qualitatively similar way as varenicline and lobeline with respect to upregulation and is subject to trapping in intracellular compartments.
claims.source: Thus, epibatidine behaves in a qualitatively similar way as varenicline and lobeline with respect to upregulation and therefore is subject to trapping in intracellular compartments, consistent with the phenomenon arising from a combination of high binding affinity for the receptor and a very basic pKa.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing pH-dependent effects on epibatidine's actions.

claims.claim: The association rate constant for 125I-epibatidine binding to α4β2Rs in living cells is 3.8 × 10^7 (M-sec)^−1.
claims.source: However, the data are consistent with a single exponential process and an association rate constant of 3.8 × 107 (M-sec)−1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), similar to previous measurements using 3H-epibatidine on isolated membrane preparations containing α4β2Rs (Whiteaker et al., 1998; Gnädisch et al., 1999; Shafaee et al., 1999) and to intact cells (Whiteaker et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The single association rate is consistent with 125I-epibatidine binding with very similar rates to all cellular α4β2Rs.
claims.source: The single association rate is consistent with 125I-epibatidine binding with very similar rates to all cellular α4β2Rs and indicates that the radioligand crosses cellular membranes rapidly enough that permeation does not significantly contribute to the binding rate (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Inferred from single exponential association kinetics.

claims.claim: The dissociation of 125I-epibatidine from α4β2R-expressing cells revealed a biphasic time course that was best fit as the sum of two exponential processes.
claims.source: Second, analysis of the dissociation of 125I-epibatidine exiting the α4β2R-expressing cells revealed a biphasic time course that was best fit as the sum of two exponential processes (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The faster dissociating component of 125I-epibatidine (~40% of the total binding) had a rate constant of 1.5 × 10^−3 sec^−1 (τ = 11.4 min).
claims.source: The faster dissociating component (τ = 11.4 min; 1.5 × 10−3 sec−1),~40% of the total binding, was similar to rates previously measured for unbinding of radio-labeled epibatidine from α4β2Rs in membrane fragments.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The slower dissociation component of 125I-epibatidine had a rate constant of 6.0 × 10^−6 sec^−1 (τ = 47 hr).
claims.source: In contrast, the slower dissociation component (τ = 47 hr) had a rate constant of 6.0 × 10−6 sec−1 and therefore was >100 fold slower than previous measurements of 125I-epibatidine unbinding from α4β2Rs.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The slow component of 125I-epibatidine dissociation was >100 fold slower than previous measurements of 125I-epibatidine unbinding from α4β2Rs.
claims.source: In contrast, the slower dissociation component (τ = 47 hr) had a rate constant of 6.0 × 10−6 sec−1 and therefore was >100 fold slower than previous measurements of 125I-epibatidine unbinding from α4β2Rs.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and comparison to literature values.

claims.claim: 0.10–0.20 pmol of 125I-epibatidine dissociated during the faster dissociation component, corresponding to a concentration of 0.2–0.4 nM free 125I-epibatidine in the assay volume.
claims.source: We found that 0.10–0.20 pmol of 125I-epibatidine dissociated during the faster dissociation component in the assay shown in Figure 4A, which corresponds to a concentration of 0.2–0.4 nM free 125I-epibatidine in our 0.5 ml assay volume of the eppendorf tube used in these assays.
claims.evidence: Calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Dissociation of 125I-epibatidine in the presence of 100 μM nicotine occurred with a much faster overall time course, such that the radioligand was released in less than a minute.
claims.source: Dissociation of 125I-epibatidine in the presence of nicotine occurred with a much faster overall time course, such that the radioligand was released in less than a minute rather than being trapped for hours.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The rapid release of 125I-epibatidine in the presence of nicotine was followed by a slower time course of dissociation (τ = 24 min at 37°C) with a rate constant of 7.0 × 10^−4 sec^−1.
claims.source: The rapid release of radioligand was followed by a slower time course of dissociation (τ = 24 min at 37°C), which is typical of rates (7.0 × 10−4 sec−1) previously measured for the dissociation of 3H-epibatidine from α4β2Rs and dissociation constants for affinity (KD = 18 pM) (Whiteaker et al., 1998; Gnädisch et al., 1999; Shafaee et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The addition of 100 nM nicotine only reduced the slow component of 125I-epibatidine dissociation by ~20%.
claims.source: We tested this prediction in additional dissociation assays and instead found that the addition of 100 nM nicotine only reduced the slow component of dissociation by ~20% (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Higher concentrations of nicotine (100 μM – 10 mM) added into the dissociation assay act on both components of the trapping phenomenon: preventing 125I-epibatidine rebinding and reducing the pH gradient to neutralize acidic compartments.
claims.source: Higher concentrations of nicotine (100 μM – 10 mM) added into the dissociation assay act on both components of the trapping phenomenon; that is, increasing nicotine concentrations not only prevented 125I-epibatidine rebinding but also reduced the pH gradient to neutralize acidic compartments, leading to deprotonation (and release) of 125I-epibatidine.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing concentration-dependent effects of nicotine on 125I-epibatidine dissociation (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: The proportion of 125I-epibatidine dissociation contributed by the slower component decreased with increasing nicotine concentrations and saturated at a value of ~60% of the total 'bound' 125I-epibatidine for both the untreated and nicotine-treated cells.
claims.source: This was evident in the fact that the proportion of 125I-epibatidine dissociation contributed by the slower component decreased with increasing nicotine concentrations and saturated at a value of ~60% of the total 'bound' 125I-epibatidine for both the untreated and nicotine-treated cells (Figure 4C), which is the entirety of the slowly dissociating component.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Chloroquine (150 μM) reduces the pH gradient of acidic compartment at similar concentrations to nicotine and has a similar effect on 125I-epibatidine binding.

results.result: Varenicline reduces nicotine-induced upregulation of α4β2 nicotinic receptors in live cells and neurons but not in membrane preparations. At 30 μM, varenicline prevented nicotine upregulation in intact cells (C1, C33, C34, C36), while in membrane preparations varenicline upregulated binding to the same degree as nicotine (C2, C49).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C33, C34, C36, and C49 are supported by experimental data from 125I-epibatidine binding assays in both HEK cells and cortical neurons (Figures 1B, 1F). The differential effects in live cells versus membrane preparations are consistently demonstrated across multiple experimental conditions.

results.result: The effects of varenicline on nicotine upregulation depend on intracellular pH homeostasis. Neutralization of acidic compartments with NH4Cl, bafilomycin A, or chloroquine eliminated varenicline's suppressive effects on nicotine upregulation (C3, C56, C57, C58, C59, C60).
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C56-C60 are well-supported by experimental data showing that multiple methods of pH neutralization (NH4Cl, bafilomycin A, chloroquine) consistently reversed varenicline's effects in both HEK cells and cortical neurons (Figures 1D, 1E, 1F, Figure 1—figure supplements 2A, 2B). The convergence of results across different pH-neutralizing agents strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Varenicline is trapped as a weak base in acidic compartments and slowly released, where it blocks 125I-epibatidine binding and desensitizes α4β2Rs. The trapped varenicline competes with epibatidine binding within acidic vesicles, while slow release desensitizes cell-surface receptors (C4, C5, C6, C122, C123, C124, C125).
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C122-C125 are supported by converging evidence from binding assays, electrophysiology, and transfer experiments (Figures 1, 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The pH-dependent effects, differential behavior in live cells versus membranes, and slow release kinetics provide strong support for the trapping mechanism.

results.result: Epibatidine itself is trapped in acidic vesicles, with direct measurement of slow release kinetics. Dissociation of 125I-epibatidine from live cells showed biphasic kinetics with a slow component (τ = 47 hr, rate constant 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ sec⁻¹) that was >100-fold slower than receptor unbinding rates (C7, C8, C92, C93, C94, C95).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, and C92-C95 are supported by detailed kinetic analysis of 125I-epibatidine dissociation (Figure 4A). The biphasic dissociation with quantified rate constants provides direct evidence for trapping. The comparison to literature values for receptor unbinding strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: 125I-epibatidine trapping requires the presence of α4β2Rs. HEK cells lacking α4β2Rs showed only ~1% of the binding observed in receptor-expressing cells, demonstrating that selective trapping does not occur without α4β2R expression (C9, C103, C104, C105, C106).
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C103-C106 are supported by experimental data comparing cells with and without α4β2Rs (Figure 4D). The minimal binding in cells lacking receptors provides strong evidence that high-affinity receptor binding is required for selective trapping.

results.result: Nicotine exposure increases epibatidine trapping by increasing the numbers of acidic vesicles containing α4β2Rs. Nicotine caused a 4-5-fold increase in trapped 125I-epibatidine (C10, C109, C110), which paralleled increased numbers of α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles visualized with pHluorin-tagged α4 subunits (C116, C118, C148).
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C109, C110, C116, C118, and C148 are supported by converging evidence from radioligand binding (Figure 4F) and fluorescence imaging (Figure 5A, B, C). The parallel increases in trapping and vesicle numbers provide strong support for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Varenicline shows concentration-dependent effects on nicotine upregulation with an inverted U-shaped dose-response curve peaking at 100 nM - 1 μM. At 100 nM, varenicline significantly reduced nicotine upregulation to ~60% for both rat and human α4β2Rs (C35, C37, C42, C44, C126).
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C37, C42, C44, and C126 are supported by dose-response data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and Figure 1G). The effects at 100 nM are particularly relevant as this concentration is estimated to occur in human brain with prescribed varenicline doses.

results.result: Lobeline, another nAChR partial agonist with smoking cessation activity, shows effects similar to varenicline. Chronic lobeline exposure reduced 125I-epibatidine binding below control levels in live cells, with an inverted U-shaped concentration-dependence peaking at ~50% of nicotine-induced upregulation at 100 nM - 1 μM (C46, C47, C48, C50, C51).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48, C50, and C51 are supported by experimental data from binding assays in both live cells and membrane preparations (Figure 1B, F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D). The parallel behavior with varenicline strengthens the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Varenicline and lobeline prevent functional upregulation of α4β2Rs measured by ACh-evoked currents. Nicotine increased peak current amplitudes ~5-fold, while varenicline and lobeline co-incubated with nicotine occluded this functional upregulation (C61, C62, C63, C64). NH4Cl treatment partly restored nicotine-induced functional upregulation (C66).
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C66 are supported by patch-clamp recordings (Figure 2A-D). The functional data parallel the binding data, providing convergent evidence. However, the restoration by NH4Cl was less complete for functional upregulation than for binding, which is noted but not fully explained.

results.result: Nicotine is not trapped in acidic compartments of α4β2R-expressing cells. Nicotine upregulation was similar in live cells and membrane preparations, and was unaffected by pH neutralization (C68, C69, C70).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by experimental data (Figures 1, 2C, D) and citation to prior work (Jia et al., 2003). The lack of pH-dependent effects for nicotine contrasts with varenicline and lobeline, supporting the differential trapping hypothesis.

results.result: DHβE, a competitive antagonist and weak base with lower pKa than varenicline, induces upregulation but is not trapped in acidic compartments. DHβE upregulated binding and currents but did not occlude nicotine upregulation, and its effects were unchanged by pH neutralization (C71-C77). This is attributed to insufficient protonation at low pH (C78).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 are supported by experimental data (Figure 3B, E) and pKa values (Table 1). The lack of pH-dependent effects for DHβE, despite being a weak base, supports the hypothesis that both high pKa and high receptor affinity are required for trapping.

results.result: Mecamylamine, a noncompetitive antagonist with very high pKa but low receptor affinity, does not show upregulation or trapping. Despite its high pKa (11.2), mecamylamine showed no evidence of upregulation or pH-dependent effects (C79, C81), suggesting that high-affinity receptor binding is required for trapping (C83).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by experimental data (Figure 3D) and affinity values (Table 1). The lack of trapping despite high pKa supports the hypothesis that both pKa and receptor affinity are required. However, the alternative explanation that mecamylamine cannot cross membranes due to high pKa is discussed but not definitively ruled out.

results.result: Epibatidine, with high pKa and high receptor affinity, behaves similarly to varenicline and lobeline. Epibatidine (30 μM) did not promote upregulation in intact cells but reduced nicotine-induced upregulation (C85, C86). With NH4Cl treatment, epibatidine upregulated binding to 60% of nicotine levels (C87, C88), demonstrating pH-dependent trapping (C89).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 are supported by experimental data (Figure 3C, D, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B) and physicochemical properties (Table 1). The pH-dependent effects for epibatidine provide strong support for the trapping mechanism based on both pKa and receptor affinity.

results.result: 125I-epibatidine binds to α4β2Rs in living cells with a single association rate constant of 3.8 × 10⁷ (M-sec)⁻¹. The single exponential association kinetics indicates that the radioligand crosses cellular membranes rapidly enough that permeation does not significantly contribute to the binding rate (C90, C91).
results.evaluation: Claims C90 and C91 are supported by kinetic analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and comparison to literature values. The single association rate is consistent with rapid membrane permeation and similar binding rates to all cellular α4β2Rs.

results.result: High concentrations of nicotine (100 μM - 10 mM) rapidly release trapped 125I-epibatidine by both preventing rebinding and neutralizing acidic compartments. Low nicotine concentrations (100 nM) only reduced the slow dissociation component by ~20% (C99), while high concentrations caused rapid release within 1 minute (C97) followed by slower unbinding (C98). The dual action prevents rebinding and reduces pH gradients (C100, C101).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 are supported by detailed dissociation experiments with varying nicotine concentrations (Figure 4B, C). The concentration-dependent effects provide insight into the mechanism of trapping and release, though the interpretation of dual action is somewhat inferential.

results.result: Nicotine upregulation does not change the relative proportions of bound versus trapped 125I-epibatidine. The fraction specifically bound to α4β2Rs remained at ~40% and the fraction trapped remained at ~60% with nicotine upregulation (C107, C108).
results.evaluation: Claims C107 and C108 are supported by dissociation kinetics data. This finding is important for understanding the mechanism of upregulation, showing that nicotine increases both pools proportionally rather than selectively increasing one pool.

results.result: Super ecliptic pHluorin (SEP)-tagged α4 subunits localize to the ER and cell surface at neutral pH, with an additional pool in acidic vesicles revealed by NH4Cl treatment. α4SEP was found throughout the ER and on the cell surface (C112, C113), with NH4Cl revealing small vesicles containing α4SEP (C114).
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 are supported by fluorescence imaging data (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The pH-sensitive properties of SEP allow visualization of receptors in acidic compartments, providing direct evidence for receptor localization.

results.result: α4β2Rs in acidic vesicles are likely mature, fully assembled receptors distributed throughout neurons. The α4SEP subunits in acidic vesicles are likely mature receptors because assembly occurs in the ER before entry into acidic compartments (C115). In neurons, α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles were found in dendrites, axons, and somata (C117).
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is supported by citation to Sallette et al., 2005 and knowledge of receptor trafficking, while C117 is supported by imaging data (Figure 5B). The inference about receptor maturity is reasonable based on the trafficking pathway, though direct evidence for assembly state is not provided.

results.result: Varenicline's effects on upregulation are independent of its partial agonist activity and require intact acidic vesicles. The effects depend on intracellular pH and trapping rather than receptor activation (C119, C120), explaining why previous studies using membrane preparations did not observe these effects (C121).
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by the pH-dependent effects and differential results in live cells versus membranes. The interpretation that effects are independent of partial agonist activity is well-supported, though the contribution of partial agonism at higher concentrations is not fully excluded.

results.result: The inverted U-shaped dose-response for trapped ligands peaks at ~1 μM, with decline at higher concentrations attributed to pH neutralization by the weak bases themselves. The decline at concentrations >1 μM is consistent with weak base effects increasing vesicular pH and increasing release rates (C128, C129). Previous brain concentration estimates likely underestimated varenicline levels by not accounting for trapping (C127).
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 are supported by dose-response data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and understanding of weak base chemistry. The interpretation of the inverted U-shape is reasonable, though alternative explanations are not fully excluded. The critique of previous concentration estimates is valid.

results.result: Pharmacokinetic differences between varenicline and nicotine are consistent with differential trapping. Varenicline has longer plasma half-life (1 day vs 2 hr), longer time to steady-state (4 days vs 2-3 hr), less metabolism (<10% vs complete in 2 hr), and larger volume of distribution (5.9 vs 2.6 L/Kg) compared to nicotine (C130-C139), consistent with varenicline trapping and slow release.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C139 are supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies (Faessel et al., 2010; Benowitz et al., 2009). The correlation between pharmacokinetic differences and trapping is reasonable, though the causal relationship is inferential and other factors could contribute to pharmacokinetic differences.

results.result: Varenicline trapping creates a high-capacity reservoir in neurons that maintains sustained drug levels, potentially explaining clinical efficacy. The reservoir maintains relatively constant varenicline concentrations that leak out and desensitize α4β2Rs, counteracting nicotine-induced functional upregulation (C140, C141).
results.evaluation: Claims C140 and C141 are speculative inferences from the experimental findings. While the trapping mechanism is well-established, the connection to clinical efficacy is hypothetical and requires clinical validation. The proposed mechanism is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Selective trapping requires both low vesicular pH and high-affinity receptor binding, with ligand pKa and receptor affinity determining trapping efficiency. The presence of α4β2Rs provides selectivity (C142), low pH is required for protonation (C143), and both high pKa and high receptor affinity are necessary (C144). Nicotine and DHβE fail to trap due to insufficient protonation (C145), DHβE also lacks sufficient affinity (C146), while epibatidine with high pKa and affinity shows trapping (C147).
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 are supported by the systematic comparison of ligands with different pKa values and receptor affinities (Table 1, Figures 1-4). The structure-activity relationship provides strong support for the proposed mechanism, though quantitative thresholds for pKa and affinity are not precisely defined.

results.result: The identity of α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles remains unclear, though they are unlikely to be late endosomes or lysosomes. It is not clear whether nicotine increases vesicle numbers or redistributes receptors to existing vesicles (C149). The vesicles are unlikely to be late endosomes or lysosomes because receptor degradation is not increased by nicotine (C150, C151).
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C151 acknowledge limitations of the current study. The exclusion of late endosomes and lysosomes is supported by citations to previous work (Vallejo et al., 2005; Darsow et al., 2005), but the positive identification of the vesicles requires further investigation.

results.result: The trapping mechanism may guide design of more effective smoking cessation drugs and could apply to other drug classes. If trapping explains varenicline's efficacy, the findings could guide drug design (C152). The mechanism may apply to other weak base ligands binding high-affinity receptors, ion channels, or transporters (C153), potentially including cessation agents for other drugs of abuse (C157).
results.evaluation: Claims C152, C153, and C157 are speculative extrapolations from the experimental findings. While the trapping mechanism is well-established for varenicline, its relevance to clinical efficacy and applicability to other drug classes requires further investigation. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work.

results.result: Background claims about tobacco use and smoking cessation treatments. Tobacco is the leading cause of preventable deaths in the US (C11), current approved treatments are nicotine replacement, bupropion, and varenicline (C12), with varenicline being most effective (C13) but achieving only ~50% quit rates (C14).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 are supported by citations to public health reports and clinical literature. These are well-established background facts that provide context for the study.

results.result: Background claims about nicotinic receptors and nicotine addiction. Nicotine binds to high-affinity nAChRs in the brain initiating addiction (C15, C16), nAChRs are pentameric Cys-loop receptors (C17, C18), with α4β2 being the most predominant subtype in mammalian CNS (C19, C20) and closely linked to addiction (C21, C22, C23).
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C23 are supported by citations to established literature. These are well-established background facts about nicotinic receptor biology and nicotine addiction.

results.result: Background claims about varenicline's mechanism as a partial agonist. Varenicline is a high-affinity partial agonist for α4β2R (C24) designed to compete with nicotine and reduce dopamine release (C25), and it does reduce acute nicotine effects on α4β2Rs and dopamine release (C26, C27).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by established pharmacological knowledge and citations. These provide the rationale for varenicline's design and known acute effects.

results.result: Background claims about nicotine upregulation. Nicotine upregulation is linked to addiction processes including sensitization and withdrawal (C28, C29), occurs when nicotine increases high-affinity binding sites (C30), and chronic varenicline induces upregulation similar to nicotine in membrane preparations (C31). Reversal of upregulation correlates with less smoking relapse (C32).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by citations to established literature. These provide important context for why the differential effects of varenicline in live cells versus membranes are significant.

results.result: Background and comparative claims about varenicline concentrations and species differences. Brain varenicline concentrations are estimated at 32-131 nM, 4-fold higher than plasma (C38, C39, C40). Previous studies found species differences in varenicline binding (C41), but the current study found no significant differences between rat and human α4β2Rs at tested concentrations (C43). Varenicline is unlikely to act as partial agonist at brain concentrations (C45).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41, C43, and C45 are supported by citations and experimental data (Figure 1G). The lack of species differences at relevant concentrations is important for translational relevance, though only three concentrations were tested.

results.result: Previous studies using membrane preparations found varenicline upregulated binding like nicotine. Previous studies found varenicline upregulated 3H-epibatidine binding to the same degree as nicotine with no effect on nicotine upregulation (C52), which were done with membrane preparations (C53).
results.evaluation: Claims C52 and C53 are supported by citations to Hussmann et al., 2012 and Turner et al., 2011. This provides important context for why the current findings in live cells differ from previous reports.

results.result: Background claims about nicotine trapping in Xenopus oocytes. Nicotine was previously described as trapped in acidic compartments of Xenopus oocytes expressing α4β2Rs, with slow release causing receptor desensitization (C54, C55).
results.evaluation: Claims C54 and C55 are supported by citation to Jia et al., 2003. This provides precedent for the trapping phenomenon, though the current study shows nicotine is not trapped in mammalian cells.

results.result: Transfer experiment demonstrates release of varenicline and lobeline from cells. 125I-epibatidine binding was highly reduced for cells receiving bathing solution from varenicline or lobeline-treated cells after NH4Cl treatment (C67).
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). This provides additional evidence for trapping and release, though the experiment is relatively simple and could benefit from additional controls.

results.result: Chloroquine has similar effects to nicotine on pH gradients and epibatidine binding. Chloroquine (150 μM), a weak base with similar molecular weight and pKa to nicotine, reduces pH gradients and has similar effects on 125I-epibatidine binding (C102).
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by experimental data (Figure 1E). This provides additional evidence that weak bases can neutralize pH gradients and affect binding, supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Background claims about other drugs as weak bases. Most drugs of abuse are weak base ligands (C154), amphetamines are weak bases that concentrate in acidic vesicles (C155), and certain antipsychotic drugs accumulate in synaptic vesicles (C156).
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 are supported by citations to Sulzer, 2011; Sulzer et al., 2005; and Tischbirek et al., 2012. These provide context for the broader relevance of weak base trapping in pharmacology.
